An MLP layer applies an affine matrix multiplication followed by fixed elementwise nonlinearities. A KAN layer instead sums learned univariate functions on edges, commonly represented with splines: $x'_j=\sum_i\phi_{ji}(x_i)$. This can make some low-dimensional functional relationships compact and inspectable, but learnable edge functions increase evaluation and parameter-management costs. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.19756)

Dense MLP operations map efficiently to mature GPU matrix-multiplication kernels with high arithmetic intensity. Spline evaluation, knot lookup, basis expansion, and less regular memory access can make KAN implementations slower despite favorable parameter counts. Performance depends on basis, kernel fusion, size, and hardware; it is not a theorem that every KAN must be slower. Benchmark matched approximation error, throughput, memory, and training cost on the actual problem.
